cards.back: It cannot be instantiated — new on it is a compile error
cards.extra: It exists to be extended. You can still declare variables of that type and hold subclass objects in them, which is what makes polymorphic collections possible.

cards.front: In Head First's phrase, what is an interface?
cards.back: A 100% abstract class — a pure contract with no implementation
cards.extra: It declares what a type can do and nothing about how. Since Java 8 it may hold default methods, but the mental model of "contract only" still explains why interfaces exist.

cards.front: How many classes can a Java class extend, and how many interfaces can it implement?
cards.extra: Single inheritance avoids the diamond problem for state. Multiple interfaces let a type promise several capabilities — Comparable, Runnable, Serializable — without sharing code.

cards.front: Every class implicitly extends which class?
cards.extra: That is where equals, hashCode, toString and getClass come from. If you do not override toString, printing an object gives a class name plus a hash.

cards.front: You store a Dog in an ArrayList<Object> and pull it out. What is the static type of the result?
cards.back: Object — and calling bark() on it will not compile
cards.extra: Everything leaves an ArrayList<Object> as Object regardless of what went in. You need a cast, and a wrong cast throws ClassCastException at runtime.

cards.front: How do you run the superclass's version of a method from an override?
cards.extra: It calls the parent implementation, skipping your override. Calling this.methodName() would re-enter your own version and usually recurse forever.

cards.front: Why prefer an interface over using Object for "any type" parameters?
cards.back: The interface states the contract, so the compiler can check the calls
cards.extra: With Object you must cast at every use and failures appear at runtime. With an interface, a type that does not implement it is rejected at compile time.

cards.front: What distinguishes an abstract class from a concrete one?
cards.back: A concrete class can be instantiated; an abstract class cannot
cards.extra: Both can hold state and implemented methods. The abstract one exists to be extended and may leave some behaviour to subclasses.

cards.front: A concrete subclass leaves one abstract method unimplemented. What happens?
cards.back: It does not compile — the subclass must implement it or be declared abstract
cards.extra: The compiler enforces the contract: you cannot produce a concrete class with holes in it.

cards.front: Why change a method's parameter from Dog[] to Animal[]?
cards.back: So one method serves every Animal subclass, not just Dogs
cards.extra: The array type is what limits reuse. The code inside works through the Animal contract, so Cats and Lions need no new method.

cards.front: A loop calls makeNoise() on a mix of Dog and Cat objects held as Animal. Why does each make a different sound?
cards.back: Each object's actual class decides which override runs
cards.extra: The array only knows they are Animals, which is enough to compile the call. At runtime the JVM dispatches to Dog's bark or Cat's meow — one loop, many behaviours.

cards.front: A class does not override toString(). What does printing its object show?
cards.back: The class name, @, and a hexadecimal hash code
cards.extra: That default comes from Object. It is an identity string, which is why logs full of Dog@1b6d3586 mean somebody forgot to override toString.
